title: Covered in, full of, -ish
summary: Suffixes that attach to nouns to describe appearance, quantity and attitude: {ずくめ}, {まみれ}, {めく}, {ぐるみ}, {じみる}, and the belittling {ごとき}.

points.title: 〜ずくめ
points.meaning: nothing but; entirely X; X from head to toe
points.explanation:
{〜ずくめ} means something consists entirely of X. It is used with a limited set of nouns:

- **Colours, especially black:** {黒[くろ]ずくめの男[おとこ]} 'a man dressed all in black'
- **Good things:** {いいことずくめ}, {おめでたいことずくめ}, {ごちそうずくめ}
- **Rules or restrictions:** {規則[きそく]ずくめ} 'rules everywhere'

Unlike {まみれ} and {だらけ}, it is often positive.

**Register:** neutral; it's used in conversation, TV and writing. {いいことずくめ} is a common everyday phrase, and {黒[くろ]ずくめ} appears often in crime reports and mystery stories.

examples.jp: 今年[ことし]はいいことずくめの一年[いちねん]だった。
examples.en: This year was nothing but good things.

examples.jp: 黒[くろ]ずくめの男[おとこ]が、店[みせ]の前[まえ]に立[た]っていた。
examples.en: A man dressed all in black was standing in front of the shop.

examples.jp: この学校[がっこう]は規則[きそく]ずくめで、息[いき]が詰[つ]まりそうだ。
examples.en: This school has rules for everything; it's suffocating.

examples.jp: 結婚[けっこん]に昇進[しょうしん]と、今年[ことし]はおめでたいことずくめだ。
examples.en: Marriage, then a promotion — this year has been one celebration after another.

points.notes: Don't overextend it: {✕間違[まちが]いずくめ} is wrong; use {間違[まちが]いだらけ}.

quiz.q: 昇進[しょうしん]、結婚[けっこん]、新居[しんきょ]の購入[こうにゅう]と、今年[ことし]は良[よ]いこと＿＿だった。
quiz.en: A promotion, marriage and a new home — this year has been full of good things.

quiz.q: 犯人[はんにん]は黒[くろ]＿＿の服装[ふくそう]をしていたという。
quiz.en: The culprit was reportedly dressed entirely in black.

points.title: 〜まみれ
points.meaning: covered in; smeared with (something dirty or unpleasant)
points.structure: Noun + まみれ (になる／だ／の + Noun)
points.explanation:
{〜まみれ} means the whole surface is covered in something, usually dirty, sticky or liquid: {泥[どろ]まみれ} (mud), {汗[あせ]まみれ} (sweat), {血[ち]まみれ} (blood), {ほこりまみれ} (dust), {油[あぶら]まみれ} (oil). It can also be used figuratively, for things that 'stick' to you and drag you down: {借金[しゃっきん]まみれ} 'up to one's ears in debt'.

**Register:** neutral and quite common in conversation, news and fiction. It's a vivid, physical word.

examples.jp: 子[こ]どもたちは泥[どろ]まみれになって遊[あそ]んでいた。
examples.en: The kids were playing and getting covered in mud.

examples.jp: 真夏[まなつ]の工事[こうじ]現場[げんば]で、作業員[さぎょういん]たちは汗[あせ]まみれで働[はたら]いていた。
examples.en: At the construction site in midsummer, the workers were drenched in sweat.

examples.jp: 事故[じこ]現場[げんば]には、血[ち]まみれの男性[だんせい]が倒[たお]れていた。
examples.en: A man covered in blood was lying at the scene of the accident.

examples.jp: 事業[じぎょう]に失敗[しっぱい]した彼[かれ]は、借金[しゃっきん]まみれの生活[せいかつ]を送[おく]っている。
examples.en: After his business failed, he's been living up to his ears in debt.

points.notes: {〜だらけ} means 'full of / lots of' and works with things that aren't spread over a surface ({間違[まちが]いだらけ}, {傷[きず]だらけ}). {まみれ} is specifically about being coated. {ほこりだらけ} and {ほこりまみれ} are both fine.

quiz.q: 雨[あめ]の中[なか]で試合[しあい]をした選手[せんしゅ]たちは、泥[どろ]＿＿になった。
quiz.en: The players who played in the rain ended up covered in mud.

quiz.q: 長年[ながねん]使[つか]われていない倉庫[そうこ]の荷物[にもつ]は、ほこり＿＿だった。
quiz.en: The goods in the warehouse, unused for years, were covered in dust.

points.title: 〜めく／〜めいた
points.meaning: to show signs of; to seem like; -ish
points.structure: Noun + めく / めいて / めいた + Noun
points.explanation:
{〜めく} turns a noun into a verb meaning 'to take on the feel of X'. Two typical uses:

- **Seasons:** {春[はる]めく}, {秋[あき]めく} — 'to start feeling like spring/autumn'. Very common in weather reports and letters.
- **Manner:** {冗談[じょうだん]めいた} (joking), {皮肉[ひにく]めいた} (sarcastic), {謎[なぞ]めいた} (mysterious), {言[い]い訳[わけ]めいた} (sounding like an excuse), {秘密[ひみつ]めいた} (secretive).

Before a noun it usually appears as {めいた}.

**Register:** somewhat written, but common in seasonal greetings, weather, literature and descriptions. It only works with a fixed set of nouns.

examples.jp: 三月[さんがつ]に入[はい]り、日差[ひざ]しもだいぶ春[はる]めいてきた。
examples.en: Now that it's March, the sunshine is starting to feel quite spring-like.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]は冗談[じょうだん]めいた口調[くちょう]で、本音[ほんね]を漏[も]らした。
examples.en: In a half-joking tone, he let slip what he really thought.

examples.jp: 謎[なぞ]めいた微笑[ほほえ]みを浮[う]かべて、彼女[かのじょ]は去[さ]っていった。
examples.en: With an enigmatic smile, she walked away.

examples.jp: 言[い]い訳[わけ]めいたことは言[い]いたくないが、事情[じじょう]を説明[せつめい]させてほしい。
examples.en: I don't want to make excuses, but please let me explain the circumstances.

points.notes: {めく} is fairly neutral; {じみる} (later in this unit) is critical. Compare {皮肉[ひにく]めいた} (a little sarcastic) and {子[こ]どもじみた} (childish, disapproving).

quiz.q: 木々[きぎ]が色[いろ]づき始[はじ]め、山[やま]もすっかり秋[あき]＿＿きた。
quiz.en: The trees have begun to change colour, and the mountains are really starting to look autumnal.

quiz.q: 上司[じょうし]の皮肉[ひにく]＿＿言[い]い方[かた]が気[き]になった。
quiz.en: My boss's somewhat sarcastic way of putting it bothered me.

points.title: 〜ぐるみ
points.meaning: the whole (family / town / company); including all of
points.explanation:
{〜ぐるみ} comes from {くるむ} 'to wrap up'. It means 'X as a whole, everybody in X included': {家族[かぞく]ぐるみの付[つ]き合[あ]い} 'a friendship between whole families', {町[まち]ぐるみで} 'the entire town together', {会社[かいしゃ]ぐるみの不正[ふせい]} 'company-wide wrongdoing'.

The nouns are groups: {家族[かぞく]}, {町[まち]}, {地域[ちいき]}, {学校[がっこう]}, {会社[かいしゃ]}, {組織[そしき]}. The idiom {身[み]ぐるみ剥[は]がされる} means 'to be robbed of everything (down to one's clothes)'.

**Register:** neutral; common in news ({組織[そしき]ぐるみの犯行[はんこう]} 'an organised crime involving the whole group') and in everyday talk about neighbours.

examples.jp: うちとお隣[となり]は、家族[かぞく]ぐるみの付[つ]き合[あ]いをしている。
examples.en: Our family and the family next door are friends with each other.

examples.jp: 町[まち]ぐるみで、ごみの削減[さくげん]に取[と]り組[く]んでいる。
examples.en: The whole town is working together to reduce rubbish.

examples.jp: 今回[こんかい]の不正[ふせい]は、会社[かいしゃ]ぐるみで行[おこな]われていた疑[うたが]いがある。
examples.en: It is suspected that this fraud was carried out company-wide.

examples.jp: 旅行先[りょこうさき]で強盗[ごうとう]に遭[あ]い、身[み]ぐるみ剥[は]がされた。
examples.en: I was robbed while travelling and lost everything I had on me.

points.notes: {〜ぐるみ} is different from {ぬいぐるみ} (stuffed toy) and {着[き]ぐるみ} (mascot costume), though they share the same 'wrapping' origin.

quiz.q: 子[こ]どもの安全[あんぜん]を守[まも]るため、地域[ちいき]＿＿でパトロールを行[おこな]っている。
quiz.en: To keep children safe, the whole community carries out patrols.

quiz.q: 警察[けいさつ]は、組織[そしき]＿＿の犯行[はんこう]と見[み]て捜査[そうさ]を進[すす]めている。
quiz.en: The police are investigating it as a crime involving the whole organisation.

points.title: 〜じみる／〜じみた
points.meaning: to smack of; to seem like (in a bad way); childish / theatrical etc.
points.structure: Noun + じみる / じみて / じみた + Noun
points.explanation:
{〜じみる} means 'to take on an (unwelcome) quality of X'. It is critical: the thing isn't really X, but it looks or feels like X, and the speaker disapproves.

Common combinations: {子[こ]どもじみた} (childish), {年寄[としよ]りじみた} (fogeyish), {芝居[しばい]じみた} (theatrical, fake), {脅迫[きょうはく]じみた} (threatening), {所帯[しょたい]じみた} (looking worn down by domestic life).

**Register:** neutral; used in both conversation and writing. {子[こ]どもじみた} is the one you'll hear most.

examples.jp: いい大人[おとな]が、そんな子[こ]どもじみたことを言[い]うな。
examples.en: You're a grown adult — don't say such childish things.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]の謝罪[しゃざい]は、どこか芝居[しばい]じみていた。
examples.en: His apology seemed somehow staged.

examples.jp: まだ二十代[にじゅうだい]なのに、年寄[としよ]りじみた服[ふく]ばかり着[き]ている。
examples.en: He's still in his twenties, but he only wears clothes that make him look like an old man.

examples.jp: 取引先[とりひきさき]から、脅迫[きょうはく]じみたメールが届[とど]いた。
examples.en: We received an almost threatening email from a client.

points.notes: Comparison: {〜っぽい} (casual, neutral), {〜めく} (neutral, signs of), {〜じみる} (critical), {〜らしい} (typical of a real X).

quiz.q: 三十歳[さんじゅっさい]にもなって、そんな子[こ]ども＿＿わがままを言[い]うものではない。
quiz.en: At thirty, you shouldn't be making such childish demands.

quiz.q: 彼[かれ]の大[おお]げさな涙[なみだ]は、芝居[しばい]＿＿いて信用[しんよう]できない。
quiz.en: His exaggerated tears seem theatrical, and I can't believe them.

points.title: 〜ごとき (the likes of)
points.meaning: the likes of; a mere (humble or contemptuous)
points.structure: Noun + ごとき (が／に／で) / Noun + ごとき + Noun
points.explanation:
{ごとき} originally means 'like, similar to' (see {ごとし} in Unit 14). After a person or thing, it has a strong evaluative meaning: 'the likes of X, a mere X'.

- **Humble (about yourself):** {私[わたし]ごとき} 'someone like me' — modest, very polite.
- **Contemptuous (about others):** {お前[まえ]ごとき} 'the likes of you', {新人[しんじん]ごときが} 'a mere newcomer'.
- **Dismissive (about things):** {風邪[かぜ]ごときで休[やす]めない} 'can't take time off for a mere cold'.

**Register:** literary and dramatic. The humble use appears in formal speech; the contemptuous use is common in manga, anime and dramas (villains love it). Be very careful using it about others in real life — it's insulting.

examples.jp: 私[わたし]ごとき者[もの]に、このような大役[たいやく]が務[つと]まるでしょうか。
examples.en: Could someone like me really fulfil such an important role?

examples.jp: 風邪[かぜ]ごときで会社[かいしゃ]を休[やす]むわけにはいかない。
examples.en: I can't take a day off work for a mere cold.

examples.jp: お前[まえ]ごときに負[ま]けるはずがない。
examples.en: There's no way I'd lose to the likes of you.

examples.jp: 新人[しんじん]ごときが、社長[しゃちょう]に意見[いけん]するなんて生意気[なまいき]だ。
examples.en: It's cheeky for a mere newcomer to voice opinions to the president.

points.notes: A softer, more common equivalent is {〜なんか／〜なんて} ({私[わたし]なんか}). {ごとき} sounds far more dramatic.

quiz.q: 私[わたし]＿＿の意見[いけん]が参考[さんこう]になるかどうか分[わ]かりませんが…。
quiz.en: I'm not sure the opinion of someone like me will be of any use, but...

quiz.q: こんな小[ちい]さなけが＿＿で、試合[しあい]を休[やす]むわけにはいかない。
quiz.en: I can't miss the match over such a minor injury.
